title: Top View of Binary Tree
problem: Imagine looking at a binary tree from directly above. Return the values of the nodes you can see, from the leftmost column to the rightmost column. For each vertical column, you see only the node closest to the top (smallest depth); if two nodes in a column are at the same depth, take the one that comes first in level order (the left one).
example: Explanation: Columns -2..2 are topped by 4, 2, 1, 3, 7. Nodes 5 and 6 sit in column 0 under 1, so they are
intuition: Give every node a horizontal distance (hd): root is 0, going left subtracts 1, going right adds 1. All nodes with the same hd are in the same vertical column. The top view is "for each hd, the node with the smallest depth".

If we traverse level by level (BFS), the first node we meet for any hd is automatically the topmost one, and ties at the same depth are resolved left-first because BFS processes each level left to right. So "first time I see this hd, record it" is all we need. The hd values always form a contiguous range (each edge changes hd by exactly 1), so we can track min and max hd and read the answer from min to max without sorting.
notes: Say it like this: "I give each node a horizontal distance: left is -1, right is +1. A DFS with a TreeMap keeping the shallowest node per column works in O(n log n). Better, a BFS meets nodes top-down and left-to-right, so the first node I see for a column is its top; with min/max tracking I avoid sorting and get O(n) time and space."
Edge cases: empty tree; a skewed tree (every node visible); two nodes at the same column and depth (left one wins).

Common mistakes: using plain DFS with putIfAbsent (DFS can reach a deep node in the left subtree before a shallower node of the same column in the right subtree, giving a wrong answer); forgetting the depth check in the DFS version; sorting when not needed.

Follow-ups: Bottom view? Same BFS, but use put (overwrite) instead of putIfAbsent, so the last node seen per column wins. Left/right view? Group by depth instead of column and take the first/last node of each level. 7.2
simple: Looking down at the tree from above, which node do you see in each column?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: DFS (preorder) the tree carrying (hd, depth).
Keep a TreeMap<hd, (depth, value)>. Replace an entry only if the new node is strictly shallower.
Preorder visits same-depth nodes left to right, so strict < keeps the left one on ties.
Read the TreeMap values in key order.
approaches.why: Each of the n nodes does a TreeMap operation costing O(log n); the map and recursion stack take O(n) in the worst case.
approaches.simple: Walk the tree remembering each node's column and depth; for each column keep the shallowest node.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: BFS from the root with a queue of (node, hd).
When a node is polled, putIfAbsent(hd, node.val): the first node seen for an hd is the top one.
Track the smallest and largest hd seen.
Output first[hd] for hd from min to max.
approaches.why: Every node is enqueued once and each HashMap operation is O(1); no sorting is needed because the hd range is contiguous. The queue and map hold up to O(n) entries.
approaches.simple: Go level by level. The first node that reaches a column is the one seen from the top.

title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, a target node in it, and an integer k, return the values of all nodes that are exactly k edges away from target. Values are unique; any order is fine. (LeetCode 863)
example: Explanation: From 5, two steps down reach 7 and 4; one step up to 3 then down to 1 also takes 2 steps.
intuition: If the tree were an undirected graph, this would be a textbook BFS: start at target, expand level by level, and the nodes at level k are the answer. The only problem is that a tree node cannot move up: it has left and right but no parent.

Fix that first: one DFS/BFS over the tree records parent[node]. Now every node has three neighbours (left, right, parent), and we BFS from target with a visited set so we never walk back the way we came. Stop after k levels; whatever is in the queue is the answer.
notes: Say it like this: "The brute force computes distance from every node to the target using LCA, which is O(n²). Instead I convert the tree into an undirected graph by storing each node's parent, then BFS from the target for k levels with a visited set. That is O(n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: k = 0 (answer is just the target); k larger than the tree height (empty list); target is the root (no parent).
Common mistakes: forgetting the visited set (you bounce between a node and its parent forever); comparing node values instead of node references when values might repeat; counting levels off by one.

Follow-ups: Can you do it without the parent map? Yes: a DFS returns the distance from each node to the target; when the target is in the left subtree at distance d, collect nodes at depth k - d - 1 in the right subtree. Still O(n) time, but O(h) extra space. Minimum Time to Burn the 7.3
simple: List every node exactly k steps away from the target node, going up or down.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Record the depth of every node.
For each node x, find LCA(x, target). The distance is depth[x] + depth[target] - 2 * depth[lca].
Collect nodes whose distance equals k.
approaches.why: We run an O(n) LCA search for each of the n nodes; the depth map and recursion stack use O(n).
approaches.simple: Compare every node with the target using their depths and lowest common ancestor to get the distance.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Traverse the tree once and store parent[child] = node.
BFS from target with a visited set. Neighbours of a node are left, right and parent.
Process the queue level by level; after k levels, the queue holds exactly the nodes at distance k.
approaches.why: Building the parent map touches each node once, and BFS visits each node at most once; the parent map, visited set and queue are O(n).
approaches.simple: Give every node a link to its parent, then treat the tree like a graph and spread out k steps from the target with BFS.

title: Minimum Time to Burn the Binary Tree from a Given Node
problem: A fire starts at the node with value start. Every minute, the fire spreads from each burning node to its left child, right child and parent. Return the number of minutes needed to burn the whole tree. Values are unique. (LeetCode 2385, "Amount of Time for Binary Tree to Be Infected")
example: Explanation: Minute 1: 1, 10, 6. Minute 2: 5. Minute 3: 4. Minute 4: 9, 2. Everything is burnt after 4
intuition: This is the previous problem in disguise. Fire spreading one edge per minute is exactly BFS from start in the undirected version of the tree. The answer is the number of BFS levels after the first one, which is the distance from start to the farthest node. So: build a parent map (also find the start node by value while doing it), then BFS level by level and count how many levels actually burn something new.
notes: Say it like this: "Fire spreading one edge per minute is BFS on the tree treated as an undirected graph. Simulating minute by minute with full scans is O(n²). Instead I build a parent map, BFS from the start node, and count levels; that is O(n) time and space."
Edge cases: single node (answer 0); start is the root; start is a leaf at the bottom of a skewed tree (answer n-1).

Common mistakes: incrementing the minute counter for the final empty level (off by one); forgetting that fire also travels upward; using values as map keys when you could use nodes (fine here since values are unique, but be explicit).

Follow-ups: Can you do it in one DFS without a parent map? Yes: the DFS returns each subtree's height, and when the start node is found it returns its (negative) distance up the chain; at each ancestor the answer is max(ans, distanceToStart + heightOfOtherSubtree). O(n) time, O(h) space. Mention it; most interviewers accept the BFS. 7.4
simple: Fire starts at one node and spreads to neighbours (parent and children) each minute. How long until it is all burnt?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Build a parent map and a list of all nodes; locate the start node.
Simulate minute by minute: scan every node; an unburnt node catches fire if its left child, right child or parent was burning before this minute.
Repeat until all nodes are burnt, counting minutes.
approaches.why: Each minute scans all n nodes, and there can be up to n minutes (a skewed tree burning from one end). Maps and sets take O(n).
approaches.simple: Simulate minute by minute, scanning every node to see if a neighbour is burning.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: One traversal builds the parent map and finds the node with value start.
BFS from that node with a visited set (neighbours: left, right, parent).
For every level, if at least one new node was burnt, add one minute.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once while building parents and once in BFS; the parent map, visited set and queue are O(n).
approaches.simple: Add parent links, then BFS from the start node. The number of BFS rounds is the time.

title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
problem: Each node has a position (row, col): root is (0, 0), the left child of (r, c) is (r+1, c-1), the right child is (r+1, c+1). Return a list of columns from left to right; inside each column, list nodes top to bottom, and if two nodes share the same row and column, put the smaller value first. (LeetCode 987)
example: Explanation: 5 and 6 are both at (2, 0), so they are sorted by value after 1 (row 0).
intuition: Every node has a key (col, row, val). The required output is just all nodes sorted by that key, then cut into groups by col. Once you see the sort order, the problem becomes: traverse once to collect triples, sort once, group.
Watch the tie rule: unlike the top view, two nodes at the same (row, col) are ordered by value, not by left/right. That is why a simple BFS order is not enough here.
notes: Say it like this: "Each node gets coordinates (row, col). Scanning the tree once per column is O(n²) in the worst case. Instead I collect (col, row, val) for every node in one traversal, sort once and group by column, which is O(n log n) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: single node; several nodes at the same (row, col) (must be sorted by value); negative values.

Common mistakes: sorting by value inside the whole column instead of only within the same row; using BFS order and forgetting the value tie-break; using a - b comparators in Java where overflow is possible (use Integer.compare).

Follow-ups: Striver's version uses TreeMap<col, TreeMap<row, PriorityQueue<val>>>; same O(n log n), more code but no explicit sort. If ties are broken by left-to-right order instead (LeetCode 314), a BFS with a column map and min/max tracking gives O(n). 7.5
simple: Report nodes column by column, top to bottom; nodes in the same spot are sorted by value.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: One DFS to find the minimum and maximum column.
For every column c from min to max, run a full DFS collecting (row, val) of nodes in that column.
Sort that column's list by row, then value, and append its values.
approaches.time: O(w·n + n log n) — O(n²) in the worst case
approaches.why: We traverse the whole tree once per column (w columns, up to n), plus the sorting; lists and recursion take O(n).
approaches.simple: Find the column range, then for each column walk the whole tree collecting its nodes.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Traverse once, recording a triple (col, row, val) for every node.
Sort all triples by col, then row, then val.
Walk the sorted list; start a new inner list whenever col changes.
approaches.why: Collection is O(n) and the single sort dominates at O(n log n); the triple list is O(n). Since the output order itself is a sorted order with value tie-breaks, O(n log n) is the practical bound.
approaches.simple: Record (column, row, value) for every node in one walk, sort them, and group by column.

title: Root to Leaf Paths in Binary Tree
problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return every path from the root to a leaf, written as values joined by "->". Any order is fine. (LeetCode 257, "Binary Tree Paths")
example: Explanation: The leaves are 5 and 3; their root paths are 1-2-5 and 1-3.
intuition: A root-to-leaf path is exactly the recursion stack of a DFS at the moment it reaches a leaf. So keep a "current path" while you go down; when you hit a leaf, record a copy; when you come back up, remove the node you added (backtracking). That way one shared buffer serves every path.
The alternative view: record every node's parent, then from each leaf walk upward to the root and reverse. It works, but it needs extra maps and walks each path a second time.
notes: Say it like this: "I can store parents and walk up from each leaf, but that needs extra maps. A DFS that keeps the current path and backtracks gives every root-to-leaf path in one traversal: O(n·h) time because of string building, O(h) extra space."
Edge cases: single node (["1"]); skewed tree (one long path); negative values (the - sign is fine with "->").
Common mistakes: forgetting to backtrack, so paths leak into each other; treating a node with one child as a leaf; recording the path at null instead of at a leaf (records each path twice).

Follow-ups: Striver's "root to node path" (path to a given value)? Same DFS, but return true once the target is found and pop only when both subtrees return false. Path Sum II? Same backtracking, carry the remaining sum. 7.6
simple: List every path from the root down to a leaf.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: BFS the tree, storing parent[child] = node, and collect all leaves.
For each leaf, follow parent pointers up to the root, collecting values.
Reverse the list and join with "->".
approaches.why: Each of up to n/2 leaves walks a path of length up to h (and the output itself has that size); the parent map and queue are O(n).
approaches.simple: Remember each node's parent, then for every leaf climb up to the root and reverse the path.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: DFS from the root with a shared StringBuilder (or array) holding the current path.
Append the current node; if it is a leaf, add the path to the result.
Recurse left and right, then undo the append (reset the length) before returning.
approaches.why: Every node is visited once, but building each answer string costs its length, so the total is bounded by the output size O(n·h). Apart from the output we only keep the recursion stack and one buffer of size O(h).
approaches.simple: Walk down with a shared path; add the node when going in, record at a leaf, remove it when coming back.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
problem: Given a binary tree and two nodes p and q in it, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree (a node counts as its own descendant). (LeetCode 236)
example: Explanation: 5 is in the left subtree of 3 and 1 is in the right subtree, so 3 is the lowest node containing
intuition: The simple idea: write down the path from the root to p and the path from the root to q. They start the same and split at some point; the last common node is the LCA.

The smarter idea asks each subtree one question: "do you contain p or q?" A recursive call returns p or q if it found one of them, or null. At a node, if the left call found something and the right call found something, this node is where the paths split, so it is the LCA. If only one side found something, pass it up. If the current node itself is p or q, return it immediately: either the other node is below it (then it is the LCA) or elsewhere (then some ancestor will see both sides).
notes: Say it like this: "The straightforward way finds root-to-p and root-to-q paths and takes the last common node: O(n) time, O(n) space, two passes. The cleaner way is one postorder pass where each call reports whether it saw p or q; the first node where both sides report something is the LCA. O(n) time, O(h) space."
Edge cases: p is an ancestor of q (answer is p); p == q; skewed tree (recursion depth n).
Common mistakes: comparing values instead of references; assuming the tree is a BST and using value comparisons; not handling the "node is p or q" case before recursing.

Follow-ups: If p or q may not exist in the tree? Count how many of them you actually found and return null unless both were seen. If it is a BST? Walk down: go left if both values are smaller, right if both are larger, else you are at the LCA, O(h). Many queries? Binary lifting gives O(log n) per query after O(n log n) preprocessing. 7.7
simple: Find the lowest node that has both p and q underneath it.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: DFS to find the root-to- p path (push, recurse, pop on failure).
Do the same for q.
Walk both paths together; the last index where they hold the same node is the LCA.
approaches.why: Each path search is a full DFS in the worst case (O(n)); the two path lists and recursion stack are O(h), up to O(n) for a skewed tree. It is correct and linear, but needs two passes and extra lists.
approaches.simple: Find the root-to-p path and the root-to-q path, then the last node they share.

e.t:
findPath(node.left, target, path) ||

e.a: node=null, target=TreeNode(1), path=[TreeNode(3), TreeNode(5), TreeNode(2), TreeNode(7)]

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: If the node is null, p or q, return it.
Recurse into left and right.
If both results are non-null, this node is the LCA; otherwise return whichever is non-null.
approaches.why: Each node is visited at most once in a single pass; the only extra memory is the recursion stack of height h.
approaches.simple: Ask both sides: if p is found on one side and q on the other, this node is the answer; otherwise pass up whatever was found.

title: Boundary Traversal of Binary Tree
problem: Return the boundary of a binary tree in anticlockwise order starting from the root: the root, then the left boundary (top-down, excluding leaves), then all leaves left to right, then the right boundary (bottom-up, excluding leaves). The left boundary starts at root.left and keeps going left when possible, otherwise right; the right boundary is the mirror. If the root has no left child, the left boundary is empty (same for right). (LeetCode 545, Premium; also on GFG)
example: Explanation: Root 1; left boundary 2 (4 is a leaf); leaves 4,7,8,9,10; right boundary bottom-up 6,3.
intuition: Split the job into three simple walks and glue them together: - Left boundary: start at root.left; at each node, add it if it is not a leaf, then move left if possible, else right. - Leaves: any traversal that visits left before right (preorder/inorder) lists leaves left to right. - Right boundary: start at root.right; move right if possible, else left; add non-leaves, but output them in reverse (bottom-up), so push them on a stack.

The only subtle part is avoiding duplicates: leaves are printed only in the leaf walk, which is why both boundary walks skip leaves, and the root is printed once at the start (unless it is itself a leaf, in which case the leaf walk prints it).
notes: Say it like this: "I break the boundary into root, left boundary without leaves, all leaves left to right, and right boundary without leaves in reverse. A lazy version collects everything and de-duplicates with a set, using O(n) extra space; doing the three walks carefully needs no set, O(n) time and O(h) space."
Edge cases: single node ([root], printed once); root with no left child (left boundary empty, do not walk into the right subtree); skewed trees.

Common mistakes: printing leaves twice (once in a boundary walk, once in the leaf walk); printing the root twice when it is a leaf; forgetting to reverse the right boundary; starting the left boundary at root instead of root.left.

Follow-ups: Can you do it iteratively? Yes: the leaf walk can use an explicit stack (push right then left). Clockwise boundary? Mirror everything: root, right boundary top-down, leaves right to left, left boundary bottom-up. 7.8
simple: Walk the outline of the tree anticlockwise: left edge, leaves, right edge (upwards).

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Collect three node lists without worrying about overlap: the full left path (including its leaf), all leaves, and the full right path (including its leaf).
Emit root, left path, leaves, then reversed right path, skipping any node already emitted (a HashSet of nodes).
approaches.why: Collecting the leaves is a full traversal; the boundary paths are O(h). The "seen" set can hold O(n) nodes, which is the cost of not thinking about overlap carefully.
approaches.simple: Collect the left edge, all leaves and the right edge separately, then remove duplicates.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Add the root if it is not a leaf.
Left boundary: from root.left, add non-leaf nodes, moving left else right.
Add all leaves with a left-first DFS.
Right boundary: from root.right, push non-leaf nodes on a stack (moving right else left), then pop them into the result.
approaches.why: The leaf DFS visits every node once; the boundary walks are O(h). Extra memory is the recursion stack plus the right-boundary stack, both O(h).
approaches.simple: Collect the three parts carefully so no node is added twice: left edge without leaves, all leaves, right edge without leaves in reverse.

title: Morris Inorder Traversal
problem: Return the inorder traversal (left, node, right) of a binary tree. The challenge version asks for O(1) extra space: no recursion and no stack. (LeetCode 94, "Binary Tree Inorder Traversal", follow-up)
example: Explanation: 1 has no left child, so print 1; then its right subtree 2 has left child 3, so print 3, then 2.
intuition: Recursion or a stack is needed only to come back to a node after finishing its left subtree. Morris traversal avoids that by temporarily creating the way back inside the tree itself.

For a node cur with a left subtree, the last node visited in that left subtree is its inorder predecessor: the rightmost node of the left subtree. That node's right pointer is null. Point it at cur (a "thread"). Now, after we finish the left subtree, following right brings us back to cur. When we arrive at cur the second time, we find the thread already pointing to cur, so we know the left side is done: remove the thread (restoring the tree), print cur, and go right.

Trace on [1,null,2,3]: cur=1 has no left, print 1, go to 2. 2 has left 3; predecessor of 2 is 3; set 3.right=2; go to 3. 3 has no left, print 3, follow 3.right to 2. At 2 the predecessor's thread points back to 2, so remove it, print 2, go right (null). Done.
notes: Say it like this: "Recursive or stack-based inorder is O(n) time and O(h) space. Morris traversal removes the stack by temporarily linking each node's inorder predecessor back to it, so we can return without a stack; we remove the link on the second visit. It is O(n) time and O(1) space, at the cost of temporarily modifying the tree."
Edge cases: empty tree; left-skewed and right-skewed trees; a single node.
Common mistakes: forgetting the pred.right!= cur condition in the predecessor loop (infinite loop); not removing the thread (the tree stays corrupted); recording the node at the wrong moment.

Follow-ups: Morris preorder? Record cur when you create the thread (and when cur.left is null) instead of when you remove it. Downside? It mutates the tree temporarily, so it is not safe if other threads read the tree concurrently. 7.9
simple: Do an in-order traversal without recursion or a stack.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Plain recursion: traverse left, add node, traverse right.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once; the call stack grows to the height h (O(n) for a skewed tree).
approaches.simple: Normal recursive in-order traversal (uses the call stack).

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: Iterative inorder with an explicit stack: keep pushing left children; when you cannot go left, pop, record, and move to the right child. Same complexity as recursion, but no risk of a call-stack overflow on deep trees, and it is the form you need for BST iterators.
approaches.why: Each node is pushed and popped once; the stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path.
approaches.simple: In-order traversal with your own stack.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: cur = root. While cur is not null:
If cur.left is null: record cur, move cur = cur.right.
Otherwise find pred, the rightmost node in cur.left (stop if pred.right == cur).
If pred.right == null: create the thread pred.right = cur, move cur = cur.left.
Else (thread exists, left subtree done): remove it pred.right = null, record cur, move cur = cur.right.
approaches.why: Finding predecessors looks expensive, but every edge is walked at most a constant number of times (about twice to create and remove each thread), so the total is O(n). We only use a few pointers; the tree is restored at the end.
approaches.simple: Morris trick: temporarily link the rightmost node of the left subtree back to the current node, so you can find your way back without a stack, and remove the link afterwards.

title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
problem: Given the root of a BST and a value that is not already in the tree, insert the value and return the root. Any valid BST is accepted; the simplest answer adds the value as a new leaf. (LeetCode 701)
example: Explanation: 5 > 4 so go right to 7; 5 < 7 and 7 has no left child, so 5 becomes 7's left child.
intuition: A search for val in a BST walks down one path, going left when val is smaller and right when it is larger. Because val is not in the tree, that search ends at a null spot, and that spot is exactly where val belongs: putting it there keeps every ancestor's ordering rule true. So insertion is "search, then attach a new leaf where the search fell off".
notes: Say it like this: "The insert position is wherever a search for the value falls off the tree. Recursively that is O(h) time and O(h) stack; iteratively it is O(h) time and O(1) space. h is log n for a balanced tree and n for a skewed one."
Edge cases: empty tree (return the new node as root); inserting a new minimum or maximum (goes to the far left or right).
Common mistakes: forgetting to return the original root; in the recursive version, not assigning the result back to root.left / root.right.

Follow-ups: Keep it balanced? That is what AVL / Red-Black trees do with rotations; Java's TreeMap is a Red- Black tree. Duplicates allowed? Pick a convention (e.g. equal goes right) and use it consistently. 7.10
simple: Insert a value into a binary search tree.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Recursive insertion: if the root is null, return a new node; otherwise recurse into the correct side and reassign the child pointer.
approaches.why: We walk one root-to-leaf path (h = log n if balanced, n if skewed), and each level adds a stack frame.
approaches.simple: Recursively go left or right until you reach an empty spot, and put the new node there.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: If the tree is empty, return a new node.
Walk down from the root with a pointer: go left if val is smaller, right otherwise.
When the next child in that direction is null, attach the new node there and stop.
approaches.why: Same single path as before, but iteration uses only one pointer instead of a call stack.
approaches.simple: Same path but with a loop and a pointer, no recursion.

title: Delete Node in a BST
problem: Given the root of a BST and a key, delete the node with that key (if it exists) and return the root of the updated BST. Any valid BST is accepted. (LeetCode 450)
example: Explanation: 3 has two children; replace it with its inorder successor 4 and remove the old 4.
intuition: Finding the node is a normal BST search. Removing it has three cases: - Leaf: just remove it (return null to the parent). - One child: let that child take its place. - Two children: we need a value that can sit in this spot and keep the ordering: the inorder successor (smallest value in the right subtree) works, because it is larger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right. Copy the successor's value into this node, then delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so that deletion is one of the easy cases.
notes: Say it like this: "Rebuilding from the inorder list works in O(n) but wastes the BST property. Instead I search for the key in O(h); a node with zero or one child is replaced by that child, and a node with two children takes its inorder successor's value, after which I delete the successor from the right subtree. Total O(h) time and space."
Edge cases: key not found (tree unchanged); deleting the root; deleting from a single-node tree (returns null).

Common mistakes: losing the subtree of the deleted node; forgetting to assign recursive results back to root.left / root.right; deleting the successor from the whole tree instead of the right subtree.

Follow-ups: Without copying values (if nodes carry other data)? Splice the successor node itself: detach it from its parent (its right child takes its place), then give it the deleted node's left and right children. Use predecessor instead? Equally valid: the max of the left subtree. 7.11
simple: Delete a key from a binary search tree and keep it valid.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Inorder-traverse the tree into a sorted list, skipping key.
Rebuild a balanced BST from the sorted list (middle element as root, recursively).
approaches.why: We visit every node and rebuild every node, and the list holds all values. It ignores the BST structure entirely, which is why it is the brute force.
approaches.simple: Read all values except the key in sorted order, then rebuild a balanced tree.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: If key < root.val, delete from the left subtree; if larger, from the right subtree.
If this is the node: if it has no left child, return its right child; if no right child, return its left child.
Otherwise find the minimum of the right subtree, copy its value here, and delete that value from the right subtree.
approaches.why: We walk one path to find the node and one more path down the right subtree to find the successor; recursion depth is at most h.
approaches.simple: Find the node. If it has one child, replace it by that child. If two, replace its value with the smallest value on its right side and delete that one instead.

title: Inorder Successor and Predecessor in BST
problem: Given a BST and a key (which may or may not be present), find the predecessor (largest value strictly smaller than key) and the successor (smallest value strictly larger than key). Return -1 for whichever does not exist. (GFG "Predecessor and Successor"; LeetCode 285 "Inorder Successor in BST" is the successor half. GFG's original signature fills Node references; here we return {pre, suc} as values.)
example: Explanation: In sorted order ... 60, (65), 70 ..., so the predecessor is 60 and the successor is 70.
intuition: Inorder of a BST is sorted, so the brute force is obvious: list it and look around the key.

But we can find each answer with one downward walk. For the successor: at a node, if node.val > key, this node is a candidate (it is bigger than key), but a smaller candidate might exist on its left, so record it and go left. If node.val <= key, everything on the left is even smaller, so go right. The last candidate recorded is the smallest value greater than key. The predecessor is the mirror image.
notes: Say it like this: "Inorder gives a sorted list, so scanning it finds both answers in O(n) time and space. Using the BST property I can walk down once per answer: for the successor, every node bigger than the key is a candidate and I move left to look for a smaller one. That is O(h) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: key smaller than every value (no predecessor); key larger than every value (no successor); key not in the tree (the strict comparisons still work); key at the root.
Common mistakes: using >= / <= and returning the key itself; stopping as soon as you find the key (the answer may be deeper in a subtree); assuming the key exists.

Follow-ups: LeetCode 285 gives a node p and asks for the successor node? Same walk using p.val, return the node. With parent pointers (LeetCode 510)? If the node has a right subtree, the successor is its leftmost node; otherwise climb parents until you come up from a left child. 7.12
simple: Find the values just before and just after a key in BST order.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Inorder traversal into a sorted list.
Scan: the last value < key is the predecessor; the first value > key is the successor.
approaches.why: We visit every node and store all values.
approaches.simple: List all values in sorted order and look around the key.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Successor: walk from the root; if node.val > key, record it and go left, else go right.
Predecessor: walk from the root; if node.val < key, record it and go right, else go left.
approaches.why: Each walk follows a single root-to-leaf path and keeps only two variables.
approaches.simple: Walk down from the root. Every time you go left, the node is a successor candidate; every time you go right, a predecessor candidate.

title: Construct BST from Preorder Traversal
problem: Given an array of distinct values that is the preorder traversal of some BST, rebuild that BST and return its root. (LeetCode 1008)
example: Explanation: 8 is the root; 5,1,7 are smaller (left subtree), 10,12 are larger (right subtree), and the same
intuition: In preorder the first value is the root. Every following value smaller than the root belongs to the left subtree, every larger value to the right. That alone gives an O(n²) or O(n log n) solution.

The O(n) idea: read the array left to right just once, and pass down an upper bound. A value can be placed in the current subtree only if it is below the bound. Building the left child of root, the bound becomes root.val; building the right child, the bound stays what it was for root. When the next value is above the bound, it does not belong here, so return null and let an ancestor take it. Each value is consumed exactly once. Trace: bound=∞ → 8 is root. Left with bound 8: 5 fits → left with bound 5: 1 fits → left with bound 1: 7 is too big, null; right of 1 with bound 5: 7 too big, null. Right of 5 with bound 8: 7 fits... and so on.
notes: Say it like this: "Inserting values one by one rebuilds the tree in O(n²) worst case. Sorting gives the inorder, and preorder + inorder builds the tree in O(n log n). The optimal way scans preorder once with an upper bound: a value goes into the current subtree only if it is below the bound, so the whole build is O(n) time and O(h) space."
Edge cases: single element; strictly increasing preorder (right-skewed tree); strictly decreasing (left-skewed).

Common mistakes: forgetting that the right child keeps the parent's bound, not the node's value; resetting the index inside recursion; using a local index variable in Java (must be a field or array so all calls share it).

Follow-ups: Is this array a valid BST preorder? Run the same bound recursion (or a monotonic stack with a running lower bound) and check that every element got consumed. From postorder? Scan from the end, build the right subtree first, and use a lower bound. 7.13
simple: Build a BST from its preorder list.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Insert each value into a BST one by one, in preorder order (inserting in preorder reproduces the same tree).
approaches.time: O(n²) worst case (O(n log n) if balanced)
approaches.why: Each insertion walks a path of length up to h, and h can be n for sorted input; the recursive insert uses O(h) stack.
approaches.simple: Insert the values one by one into an empty BST.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: The inorder of a BST is just the sorted values. Sort a copy to get the inorder, then use the classic "build tree from preorder + inorder" recursion with a value-to-index map.
approaches.why: Sorting costs O(n log n); the build is O(n) with the index map. The map and sorted array use O(n).
approaches.simple: Sort a copy to get inorder, then rebuild from preorder and inorder.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Keep a global index into preorder.
build(bound): if the index is at the end or preorder[idx] > bound, return null.
Otherwise create a node from preorder[idx++], build its left with bound node.val, its right with the same bound, and return it.
Start with bound = +∞.
approaches.why: Every value is consumed exactly once and each call does O(1) work besides recursing; the recursion depth is the tree height.
approaches.simple: Read preorder once, passing an upper bound: a value goes in this subtree only if it is below the bound.

title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
problem: Given the root of a BST and an integer k, return true if two different nodes in the tree have values that add up to k. (LeetCode 653)
intuition: On a sorted array, Two Sum is the classic two-pointer trick: one pointer at the smallest value, one at the largest; if the sum is too small move the left pointer up, if too big move the right pointer down. The inorder of a BST is that sorted array, so we can copy it out and run two pointers.

To avoid the O(n) copy, simulate the two pointers directly on the tree with two BST iterators: a normal one that yields values in ascending order (stack of left spines) and a reverse one that yields descending order (stack of right spines). Each iterator holds only O(h) nodes at a time.
notes: Say it like this: "For each node I could binary-search the complement, O(n·h). Since inorder is sorted, copying it and using two pointers is O(n) time and O(n) space. To save memory I run the two pointers directly on the tree with an ascending and a descending BST iterator, which keeps O(n) time and drops space to O(h)."
Edge cases: single node (false, you cannot use the same node twice); k equal to twice a node's value (still needs two different nodes); negative values.

Common mistakes: pairing a node with itself (the i < j check or other!= node prevents it); calling next() on an exhausted iterator (the i < j loop condition guarantees there is always a next element); integer overflow in i + j for extreme inputs.

Follow-ups: Design the BST iterator alone (LeetCode 173)? Exactly the ascending class above, with a hasNext() that checks the stack. Three sum in a BST? Fix one value with an outer traversal and run this two-pointer routine for the rest, O(n²). 7.14
simple: Is there a pair of values in the BST that sums to k?

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Traverse every node x.
Search the BST for k - x.val; it counts only if found at a node other than x.
approaches.why: Each of the n nodes triggers one O(h) BST search; the recursion stack is O(h).
approaches.simple: For each node, search the BST for its partner.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: Inorder into a sorted list, then two pointers from both ends. (A HashSet of seen values during any traversal also works in O(n) / O(n) and does not even need the BST property.)
approaches.why: One traversal plus one linear two-pointer scan; the list holds all n values.
approaches.simple: In-order gives a sorted list; use two pointers on it.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Build an ascending iterator (push the left spine) and a descending iterator (push the right spine).
i = asc.next(), j = desc.next().
While i < j: if i + j == k return true; if the sum is smaller, i = asc.next(), else j = desc.next().
Return false when the pointers meet.
approaches.why: Each node is pushed and popped at most once per iterator, so the total work is O(n) (each next() is O(1) amortized). Each stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path.
approaches.simple: Run two iterators at once, one giving the smallest values and one the largest, and move them like two pointers.

title: Recover Binary Search Tree
problem: Exactly two nodes of a BST had their values swapped by mistake. Fix the tree in place without changing its structure. (LeetCode 99)
example: Explanation: 3 cannot be the left child of 1 because 3 > 1. Swapping 1 and 3 makes it a valid BST.
intuition: The inorder of a valid BST is strictly increasing. Swapping two values creates "drops" where prev > current: - If the swapped values were not adjacent in inorder, e.g. 1 2 3 4 5 → 1 5 3 4 2, there are two drops: 5>3 and 4>2. The wrong nodes are the first node of the first drop (5) and the second node of the second drop (2). - If they were adjacent, e.g. 1 2 3 → 1 3 2, there is only one drop 3>2, and the wrong nodes are its two sides.

So during one inorder pass we keep prev and record: at the first drop first = prev, middle = current; at a second drop last = current. At the end swap first with last if a second drop exists, otherwise with middle.
notes: Say it like this: "Collecting, sorting and writing values back is O(n log n). Better: inorder should be increasing, so I find the drops in one pass. Two drops means swap the first node of the first drop with the second node of the second drop; one drop means the two nodes were adjacent. That is O(n) time, O(h) space, and with Morris traversal O(1) space."
Edge cases: swapped nodes adjacent in inorder (only one drop); one of the swapped nodes is the root; two-node tree.
Common mistakes: only handling the two-drop case (fails 1 3 2); swapping nodes instead of values (the problem says keep the structure); updating prev before the comparison.

Follow-ups: Why not just validate and swap the first two bad nodes? Because in the two-drop case the second wrong node is the right side of the second drop, not the left. What if more than two nodes were misplaced? Then the sort-and-write-back approach is the general fix. 7.15
simple: Two nodes of a BST were swapped by mistake. Fix it.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Inorder-traverse and collect all values.
Sort them.
Inorder-traverse again, writing the sorted values back into the nodes in order.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the value list is O(n).
approaches.simple: Collect values, sort, and write them back in in-order.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: One recursive inorder pass tracking prev, first, middle, last as explained above; swap at the end.
approaches.why: A single traversal; only the recursion stack is used.
approaches.simple: In-order walk, finding the two places where the order goes down; swap those two nodes' values.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Run the same drop detection on top of Morris inorder traversal (7.8): wherever Morris "visits" a node, do the prev check. This is LeetCode's O(1)-space follow-up.
approaches.why: Morris walks each edge a constant number of times and uses only pointers; the tree is restored by the time the loop ends.
approaches.simple: Same idea but with Morris traversal, so no extra space.

title: Largest BST in Binary Tree
problem: Given a binary tree, return the number of nodes in its largest subtree that is a valid BST. A subtree here means a node together with all of its descendants. (LeetCode 333 "Largest BST Subtree", Premium; GFG "Largest BST")
example: Explanation: The subtree rooted at 5 (nodes 5, 1, 8) is a BST of size 3. The whole tree is not a BST because
7 is the right child of 15 (7 < 15), and it is also in 10's right subtree (7 < 10).
intuition: A subtree rooted at node is a BST exactly when: 1. its left subtree is a BST, its right subtree is a BST, and 2. max(left subtree) < node.val < min(right subtree).

So if every child reports three numbers — its min, its max and its size if it is a BST — the parent can decide in O(1). That calls for postorder (children first). If a subtree is not a BST, it reports an impossible range (min = -∞, max = +∞) so every ancestor check fails automatically, and it passes up the best size found below it. An empty subtree reports min = +∞, max = -∞, size 0, which makes any check pass.
notes: Say it like this: "Checking every subtree with a bounds-based BST validation is O(n²). Instead I go bottom-up: each subtree returns its min, max and BST size, so a parent decides in O(1) whether it extends a BST; an invalid subtree returns an impossible range so all ancestors fail. That is O(n) time and O(h) space."
Edge cases: empty tree (0); whole tree is a BST (n); every subtree with 2+ nodes invalid (answer 1, a single leaf); duplicate values (a strict BST rejects them).

Common mistakes: only comparing a node with its direct children (the BST rule is about whole subtrees); forgetting to pass the best size up from an invalid subtree; sentinel overflow when node values hit the int limits.

Follow-ups: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree (LeetCode 1373)? Same postorder, but return the sum instead of the size and track the best sum (treat an empty BST as sum 0). Return the root of the largest BST? Return the node alongside the size.
simple: Find the size of the biggest subtree that is a valid BST.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every node, check whether its subtree is a BST using the bounds method (low < val < high).
If it is, count its nodes and update the best answer.
approaches.why: The validity check and count are O(subtree size) for each of the n nodes, which adds up to O(n²) for a skewed tree. Recursion takes O(h).
approaches.simple: For every node, check its whole subtree with the range method and count it.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Postorder: each call returns {min, max, size} for its subtree.
Null returns {+∞, -∞, 0}.
At a node with children results L and R: if L.max < node.val < R.min, it is a BST: return {min(L.min, val), max(R.max, val), L.size + R.size + 1}.
Otherwise return {-∞, +∞, max(L.size, R.size)} so no ancestor can be a BST, while still carrying the best size seen.
The answer is the size returned for the root.
approaches.why: Each node is processed once with O(1) work after its children return; the recursion stack is O(h). We use long sentinels so that node values equal to Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE do not clash with the infinities.
approaches.simple: Bottom-up: each subtree reports its min, max and size. A node is a BST if left max < node < right min.
